summary.text: Expected value, also called expectation or the mean, is a generalization of the weighted average.
When it is finite, it can be read as the long-run average of results from independent repetitions of the same random experiment.
It grew out of the problem of points, a puzzle about how to fairly divide stakes between two players forced to end a game early.

items.prompt: A friend offers a game: flip a fair coin, win $10 on heads and nothing on tails. What is the expected value of one flip?
items.explain: For finitely many values, the expected value adds each value times its probability: half of $10 plus half of $0.

items.prompt: You play the same game of chance thousands of times, each play independent of the others. What does your average result per play drift toward?

options.label: The game's expected value
The single biggest prize on offer
The most recent result you got
The smallest payout the game allows

items.explain: The expected value can be read as the long-run average of independent repetitions of the same experiment.

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die has six faces, each equally likely. How is its expected value built from the faces?

options.label: From the face that comes up most often
From the faces added up with no weights
From the middle face printed on the die
From each face weighted by its probability

items.explain: For finitely many values, the expected value is the weighted average of those values, with their probabilities as weights.

items.prompt: A spinner lands on 1 nine times out of ten and on 100 one time in ten. Why is its expected value not simply the midpoint of 1 and 100?

options.label: Because the two values are too far apart to average
Because likelier outcomes get more weight than unlikely ones
Because rare outcomes are ignored when averaging
Because expected values must be whole numbers

items.explain: Each value is weighted by its probability, so the common outcome counts for more than the rare one.

items.prompt: Two players must stop a game early, and one has a much better chance of winning it. What principle did the early thinkers use to split the stakes fairly?

options.label: Each share should be proportional to that player's chance of winning
Split the stakes equally since the game was left unfinished
Give everything to whoever is ahead right now
Return each player's own stake and divide nothing

items.explain: Pascal and Fermat held that the value of a future gain should be directly proportional to the chance of getting it.

items.prompt: Pascal and Fermat solved the same puzzle by different calculations yet got identical results. What best explains this?

options.label: They agreed beforehand which answer to reach
They tested it by playing the game many times
Both relied on one idea: gain scales with chance
They averaged all the outcomes with equal weight

items.explain: Their computations differed, but both rested on the same principle that a future gain's value is proportional to its chance.

paragraphs.heading: A weighted average
paragraphs.text: The expected value of a random variable generalizes the weighted average. It also goes by the names expectation, mean or first moment. When the variable takes only finitely many values, it is exactly that average, with each value weighted by its probability. More generally it is defined as a Lebesgue integral of the variable with respect to the underlying probability measure. It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX.

paragraphs.heading: The long run
paragraphs.text: When it is finite, the expected value can be read as the long-run average you would get from repeating the same random experiment independently. The law of large numbers is what turns that reading into a precise statement.

paragraphs.heading: The basic formula
paragraphs.text: Suppose X has a finite list of possible outcomes x₁,..., xₖ, with probabilities p₁,..., pₖ. Then E [X] = x₁p₁ + x₂p₂ + ⋯ + xₖpₖ. Because the probabilities must add up to 1, it is natural to read this as a weighted average of the outcomes.

paragraphs.heading: Born from a game
paragraphs.text: The idea grew in the mid-17th century out of the problem of points: how to split the stakes fairly when two players must stop a game early. In 1654 the Chevalier de Méré brought the problem to Blaise Pascal, who took it up in letters with Pierre de Fermat. Working independently, they reached identical results by different calculations, resting on one principle. A future gain should be valued in direct proportion to the chance of getting it. They did not publish, and told only a small circle of friends in Paris.

paragraphs.heading: Into print
paragraphs.text: Christiaan Huygens published a treatise on probability, "De ratiociniis in ludo aleæ", in 1657, soon after visiting Paris. It solved the problem of points on the same principle and added rules for harder cases, such as games with three or more players. The book can be seen as the first successful attempt to lay the foundations of probability theory. Later, in the mid-1800s, Pafnuty Chebyshev was the first person to think in a systematic way about the expectations of random variables.

paragraphs.heading: Many settings, one idea
paragraphs.text: The original definition handles finitely many outcomes, such as the flip of a coin. Infinite series stretch it to countably many outcomes, and it is also widely used for variables governed by continuous probability density functions. Measure theory and Lebesgue integration join all these cases as special cases of one general definition. It even extends to random vectors and random matrices, taken one component at a time.
